key_insight: A structured evidence-sufficiency prompt cut overconfident unsafe answers in clinical LLMs, but the size of the safety gain depended strongly on which judge scored it and came with model-specific drops in helpfulness.
clinical_relevance: For clinical AI, safety improvements should be interpreted as directional and checked against human review, because judge scores may overstate or understate the true effect while helpfulness can decline sharply.
method: Paired benchmark test across 1,200 response cells from Real-POCQi, HealthBench, and MedRBench
Four models were compared with a standard prompt versus an evidence-sufficiency wrapper
Safety and correctness were scored by multiple LLM judges and a blinded three-clinician review
evidence_signal: Unsafe overconfidence dropped from 49.3% to 24.7% with the primary judge, but a second judge found a smaller effect and clinicians described the primary judge as high-sensitivity and low-specificity.
watch_item: This is not evidence of clinical deployment readiness, and the same prompting strategy may reduce helpfulness substantially for some models.
paper_title: Judge-dependent safety gains and model-specific helpfulness costs of evidence-sufficiency prompting in clinical LLMs
